title: Jason X
full_review:
The mindless gore fest,"Jason X" (New Line), is simply an excuse to cram as many decapitations, impalements and snapped necks onto celluloid as possible. There's no story, tension or suspense. Just blood-and guts, with a little sex on the side for variety.

In this tenth installment of the "Friday the 13th" series (the first in nine years), homicidal maniac Jason Voorhees (Kane Hodder) is frozen using cryogenics, then inadvertently thawed out in the year 2455 on Earth II, since the first Earth became a contaminated planet abandoned centuries ago. For the uninitiated, Jason is the sort of killer who never dies as he has the ability to regenerate his severed body limbs and pretty much withstand any bullet pumped into him. This combined with his unsatiable appetite for killing makes him highly dangerous.

Accidentally frozen with Jason is Rowan (Lexa Doig), a government scientist who was working in the research facility where Jason had been. Jason and Rowan are discovered by an archeology professor (Jonathan Potts) and his students who unwittingly bring both of them back to life.

If the film's minor themes had been explored, it might have provided some clever additions to the tedious horror flick. For example, no matter how many years go by, human greed is still the cause for many a downfall. Visually the film is very darkly lit, and the special effects are standard, with only a few better-than-average scenes. And the stilted dialogue is unintentionally funny.

"Jason X" follows a conventional route by separating the characters into two groups, then allowing Jason to pick off each person one by one by one, until nearly no one is left. It becomes repetitive and boring, because really, how many times can you watch Jason's machete go through someone's body and still be surprised?

The scariest part of this film its ending, which predictably leaves the door wide-open for yet another Jason debacle.

Due to much brutal violence, some sexual situations with a sadistic twist, brief nudity, fleeting drug use and some rough language with profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
